title: The MRI That Finds Everyone Abnormal — Imaging The Back — 2026-09-11
rationale: This deep-dive rather than debate format suits the material because the real tension isn't two camps shouting past each other — it's one coherent argument (imaging finds things that were never going to matter, and routine use doesn't help and may harm) running into one hard exception (cauda equina, where a low positive rate is the acceptable cost of not missing a surgical emergency) and one unresourced system (NHS EDs told to raise their MRI threshold with no matching MRI access). The six sources build that arc in order: Chou and Jarvik supply the RCT-level verdict that routine/early imaging doesn't improve outcomes and can tilt toward more surgery; First10EM supplies the overdiagnosis mechanism that explains why an incidental finding becomes a label a patient can't un-hear; St Emlyn's and EM Cases pin down what a defensible emergency indication actually looks like in a UK ED — an 11.1% positive rate for suspected CES and the PVR/CT workarounds used when MRI isn't sitting empty at 3am; and the RCEM position statement supplies the honest institutional friction — the college agrees with the clinical logic of the national CES pathway but refuses to endorse it because nobody funded the scanners to match the lowered threshold. Brinjikji's asymptomatic-prevalence review opens the episode; the LIRE trial's mixed report-nudge result is background context the hosts can mention, though no independently verifiable URL for it made the cut here. Together these sources let the hosts trace one throughline — the same statistical fact (degenerative findings are near-universal with age) that makes routine imaging low-yield is what makes CES scanning's low positive rate defensible, not damning — without staging a manufactured fight where none of the source material actually disagrees.
case_vignette: A 34-year-old office worker walks in with three weeks of axial low back pain, no red flags, and asks for "the scan" because a colleague's MRI "found the cause" of their back pain last year. Two bays down, a 58-year-old presents with two days of bilateral leg pain, saddle-area numbness, and new difficulty starting his stream — and the question is no longer whether to scan, but how fast an MRI (or, if the scanner isn't free, a bridging CT) can happen. Same modality, same department, same night shift — and the entire episode lives in why one of these patients should almost certainly not get an MRI and the other cannot leave without one.

sources.title: Brinjikji et al., Systematic literature review of imaging features of spinal degeneration in asymptomatic populations (AJNR, 2015) — abstract
sources.why: The opening fact: disc degeneration, bulges and protrusions are present in a large and age-rising share of people with no back pain at all, so a report listing them is describing age, not necessarily the cause of the pain in front of you.

sources.title: Chou et al., Imaging strategies for low-back pain: systematic review and meta-analysis (Lancet, 2009)
sources.why: The trial-level verdict: pooled RCTs show immediate lumbar imaging for low back pain without red flags changes pain, function, or quality of life not at all — this is the evidence NICE NG59's 'do not routinely image' rests on.

sources.title: Jarvik et al., Rapid MRI vs radiographs for low back pain (JAMA, 2003)
sources.why: The head-to-head RCT that makes the harm concrete: rapid MRI produced equivalent outcomes to plain films at one year, at higher cost and with a trend toward more spine surgery — imaging itself nudging the treatment pathway.

sources.title: Overdiagnosis: Would we be better off not looking? — First10EM
sources.why: Supplies the mechanism connecting Brinjikji's asymptomatic-findings data to real harm: a true-positive finding that would never have caused illness still gets labelled, and 'the genie can't go back in the bottle' once a patient is told their MRI found something.

sources.title: Re-evaluating risk factors for Cauda Equina — St Emlyn's
sources.why: Gives the actual UK number for the defensible side: 11.1% MRI-confirmed cauda equina compression in a UK tertiary series — the empirical price tag for 'we scan a lot of negatives so we don't miss the one positive,' plus candid detail on which red flags actually predict compression.

sources.title: Ep 222 Imaging Decisions in Emergency Medicine — EM Cases
sources.why: The current FOAMed articulation of what UK EDs do when MRI isn't immediately available — PVR thresholds and CT lumbar spine as interim risk-stratification for suspected CES — showing the practical workaround to the access gap RCEM flags.

sources.title: RCEM Position Statement: Cauda Equina Syndrome (2024)
sources.why: The genuine institutional tension: RCEM won't formally endorse the national CES pathway because it lowers the MRI-request threshold without funding the 24/7 MRI access to meet it — evidence-based indication colliding with unresourced infrastructure, which is exactly why NG59 is hard to follow in practice.
